'''Simon Mawer''' ({{IPAc-en|m|ɔːr}} {{respell|MOR}}; 18 September 1948 – 12 February 2025) was a British author who lived in Italy.<ref name="death">{{cite web|first=Heloise|last=Wood|url=https://www.thebookseller.com/news/wonderful-simon-mawer-dies-unexpectedly-aged-76|title='Wonderful' Simon Mawer dies unexpectedly aged 76|magazine=The Bookseller|date=17 February 2025|accessdate=17 February 2025}}</ref>

==Early life and work==
Born in England and educated at [[Millfield School]] in Somerset and at [[Brasenose College, Oxford]], Mawer took a degree in zoology and worked as a biology teacher for most of his life. He published his first novel, ''Chimera'', (Hamish Hamilton, 1989) at the comparatively late age of forty-one. It won the [[McKitterick Prize]] for a first novel by an author over the age of forty. ''Mendel's Dwarf'' (1997) followed three works of modest success and established him as a writer of note on both sides of the Atlantic.{{citation needed|date=April 2012}} ''[[The New York Times]]'' described it as a "thematically ambitious and witty novel".<ref name="NYT Chromosomal">{{cite news|last=Prose|first=Francine|title=Get Out the Chromosomal Map|url=https://www.nytimes.com/books/98/03/22/reviews/980322.22proset.html|accessdate=15 July 2012|newspaper=The New York Times|date=22 March 1998}}</ref> [[Uzo (filmmaker)|Uzo]] optioned film rights, and then later [[Barbra Streisand]] optioned them.

The novels ''The Gospel of Judas'' (2000) and ''The Fall'' (2003) came next, followed by ''Swimming to Ithaca'' (2006), a novel partially inspired by his childhood on the island of [[Cyprus]]. He then published another non-fiction book, ''Gregor Mendel: Planting the Seeds of Genetics'' (2006), published in conjunction with the [[Field Museum]] of Chicago as a companion volume to the museum's concurrent exhibition of the same name.

In 2009 he published ''[[The Glass Room]]'', a novel about a modernist villa [[Villa Tugendhat|Tugendhat]] built in a Czech city. His 2012 book ''[[The Girl Who Fell from the Sky]]'' (''Trapeze'' in the US) was received positively on both sides of the Atlantic, described as "a professionally crafted and engaging story"  and a "skillfully and intelligently executed thriller".<ref name="WashPost June2012">{{cite news|last=Smith|first=Wendy|title='Trapeze,' by Simon Mawer|url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/entertainment/books/trapeze-by-simon-mawer/2012/06/11/gJQAs5mbVV_story.html|accessdate=15 July 2012|newspaper=The Washington Post|date=11 June 2012}}</ref> In 2015 he published ''Tightrope'', a follow-on to ''The Girl Who Fell from the Sky.''  ''Tightrope'' has been described as "...skillful and evocative examination of a mind under stress. Most recently, he wrote ''Prague Spring'' (2018) about Brits living in and travelling through Czechoslovakia during both the [[Prague Spring]] and subsequent [[Warsaw Pact invasion of Czechoslovakia|Warsaw Pact invasion]].

==Personal life and death==
Mawer lived in Rome from 1977, teaching [[biology]] at [[St. George's British International School]] in Rome. He was married with two children.<ref>{{cite web|title=The Glass Room: Author Biography|url=http://www.themanbookerprize.com/prize/books/392|publisher=The Man Booker Prize|accessdate=15 July 2012|url-status=dead|archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20120610111038/http://themanbookerprize.com/prize/books/392|archivedate=10 June 2012}}</ref> Mawer died on 12 February 2025, at the age of 76.<ref name="death"/>

==Awards and honours==
*1990 [[McKitterick Prize]] for first novels, ''Chimera''
*2003 [[Boardman Tasker Prize for Mountain Literature]], ''The Fall''
*2003 [[Man Booker Prize]], longlist, ''The Fall''
*2009 [[Man Booker Prize]], shortlist, ''The Glass Room''<ref>{{cite web|url=https://news.bbc.co.uk/2/hi/entertainment/arts_and_culture/8243551.stm|title=Man Booker shortlist is announced|access-date=8 September 2009|date=8 September 2009|work=BBC News}}</ref>
*2010 [[Walter Scott Prize]], shortlist, ''The Glass Room''<ref>[https://www.theguardian.com/books/2010/apr/01/booker-rivals-walter-scott-prize-shortlist "Booker rivals clash again on Walter Scott prize shortlist"], ''The Guardian'', 2 April 2010</ref>
*2016 [[Walter Scott Prize]], winner, ''Tightrope''<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.walterscottprize.co.uk/simon-mawer-wins-2016-walter-scott-prize/ |title=The winner of the 2016 Walter Scott Prize is announced! |publisher=Walter Scott Prize  |date=18 June 2016 |accessdate=20 June 2016}}</ref>
